a: When Jesus finished all these words
p: Matthew closes each of Jesus' five long speeches this way. This time he adds "all."
b: Matthew ends each of Jesus' five great speeches with the same line (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1). Here, after the speech on the Mount of Olives (chapters 24–25), he adds one word: "all these words." The teaching is complete, and the story turns to the cross. Many readers hear an echo of Moses, who "finished speaking all these words to all Israel" just before his death (Deuteronomy 32:45). Matthew often shapes Jesus' story to recall Moses: a teacher who gives God's will from a mountain and then dies with his people's future in view. Some scholars count five speeches to match the five books of Moses, though that link is debated.

p: Passover remembered the escape from Egypt. Pilgrims crowded Jerusalem, and Roman soldiers watched them closely.
b: Passover (Hebrew Pesach) remembered the night God spared Israel's firstborn and brought the people out of Egypt (Exodus 12). The lambs were slaughtered at the Temple on the afternoon of 14 Nisan and eaten that night, the start of 15 Nisan, which also began the seven-day Feast of Unleavened Bread (Deuteronomy 16:1–8). Pilgrims came from everywhere. Josephus gives enormous numbers, surely inflated, but the city may have swelled to several times its normal size. A feast about freedom from a foreign king, held under Roman rule, was tense: the governor came up from Caesarea with extra troops. Jesus ties his death to this feast on purpose.

p: The same Greek verb is used for Judas, the priests, Pilate and God's plan. This translation keeps it as "hand over."
b: The verb paradidōmi means "hand over, deliver up." Most English Bibles say "betray" when Judas does it and "deliver" or "hand over" for everyone else. The Greek uses one word all through the passion: Judas hands Jesus over to the priests (26:15–16), the priests hand him over to Pilate (27:2, 18), and Pilate hands him over to be crucified (27:26). Behind them all stands God's purpose: the Greek of Isaiah 53:12 says the servant "was handed over because of their sins," and Paul says God "handed him over for us all" (Romans 8:32). This translation keeps "hand over" every time so readers can follow the chain. Here the present tense ("is being handed over") treats the event as already under way.

p: Joseph Caiaphas held the office from about AD 18 to 36, longer than anyone else under Roman rule.
b: Josephus calls him "Joseph who was called Caiaphas" and says the Roman governor Valerius Gratus appointed him; Vitellius removed him around AD 36 or 37 (Josephus, Antiquities 18.35, 95). Holding office for eighteen years under Rome meant working closely with Pilate, who governed for ten of those years. In 1990 a family tomb was found south of Jerusalem with an ornate bone box inscribed "Joseph son of Caiaphas." Many scholars think it held the high priest's bones, though some doubt the identification. John 18:13 adds that Annas, his father-in-law and an earlier high priest, still had great influence.

p: Passover crowds had rioted before. The leaders wanted Jesus quietly removed, but events overtook their plan.
b: Josephus describes riots at the festivals. Under the governor Cumanus (about AD 48–52), a soldier's insult at Passover set off a panic in which, Josephus says, thousands died (Jewish War 2.224–227). A popular prophet from Galilee, cheered by pilgrims a few days earlier (21:9–11), was dangerous at such a time. The irony in Matthew is plain: the leaders decide "not at the festival," but Judas's offer changes their timing, and Jesus dies at Passover after all, as he has just said (26:2). The word for "uproar" (thorybos) returns at 27:24: the uproar the leaders feared does break out, but it is aimed at Jesus.

a: Simon, the man with the skin disease
p: The Greek lepros covered many skin conditions. Simon was probably known by the name after he was healed.
b: Older Bibles say "Simon the leper." The Greek lepros, like the Hebrew tsara'at behind it (Leviticus 13), covered many visible skin diseases, not only what doctors now call leprosy (Hansen's disease). A man with an active case could not host a dinner party, so Simon had probably been healed, perhaps by Jesus (compare 8:2–4; 11:5), and kept the nickname. Matthew and Mark name him; John 12:1–8 sets a similar anointing in the home of Lazarus, Martha and Mary, also in Bethany, and Luke 7:36–50 tells of a woman who anoints Jesus in the house of a Pharisee also named Simon.

a: she poured it over his head
p: Oil on the head was how Israel made kings. Jesus says this anointing is for his burial.
b: In Israel, prophets poured oil on the heads of kings (1 Samuel 10:1; 1 Samuel 16:13; 2 Kings 9:6), and "Messiah" means "anointed one." A woman anointing Jesus' head days before he is hailed as "King of the Jews" on a cross looks like a royal anointing done in secret. Jesus gives it another meaning: she has prepared his body for burial (26:12). Both can be true in Matthew: the king is anointed for a throne that is a cross. In John 12:3 Mary anoints his feet. The perfume (Mark 14:5 and John 12:5 put it at three hundred denarii, about a year's wages for a laborer) shows extravagant devotion.

p: Matthew blames "the disciples"; Mark says "some"; John names Judas.
b: The three accounts give the complaint to different people. Mark 14:4 says "some" were angry. Matthew makes it "the disciples," which fits his frank picture of the Twelve in the passion: they sleep, flee and deny. John 12:4–6 names Judas and adds that he stole from the common purse. Matthew places Judas's visit to the priests right after this scene (26:14), which suggests a link without saying it.

a: you have the poor among you at all times
p: Jesus echoes Deuteronomy, which says the poor will always be there and so you must open your hand.
b: This line is often quoted as if Jesus accepted poverty as normal. He is echoing Deuteronomy 15:11: "For there will never stop being people in need in the land. That is why I am commanding you: Open your hand wide to your brother, to the poor and the needy among you in your land." The point is not that the poor do not matter, but that there will always be time to help them, while this moment with Jesus is about to end. Matthew's Jesus elsewhere makes care for the poor the test of the final judgment (25:31–46) and tells the rich man to sell and give (19:21).

p: Jesus promises the woman a memorial wherever the good news goes, yet Matthew never gives her name.
b: "For a memorial of her" uses the word for a reminder before God (the same word is used of offerings in the Greek Old Testament). The promise has come true, yet in Matthew and Mark she has no name. John 12:3 calls her Mary of Bethany. Later Western tradition merged her with Mary Magdalene and with the sinful woman of Luke 7, though the Gospels do not say so; Eastern churches kept them apart, and Catholic teaching since 1969 no longer joins them in the liturgy. The feminist scholar Elisabeth Schüssler Fiorenza titled her landmark book In Memory of Her (1983) from this verse, arguing that the church kept the story but forgot the woman.

p: Iscariot may mean "man from Kerioth." The Gospels give money, Satan and disappointment as motives.
b: "Iscariot" is most often explained as Hebrew ish Qeriyyot, "man of Kerioth," a town in Judea, which would make Judas the one Judean among Galileans. Other proposals: from sicarius, "dagger man," a name for Jewish rebels; or from an Aramaic word for "false." His motive is never fully explained. Matthew alone has him ask for money (26:15). Luke 22:3 and John 13:2, 27 say Satan entered him. Some modern writers suggest he was disappointed that Jesus would not lead a revolt, or tried to force his hand, but the Gospels say nothing of this. The second-century Gospel of Judas, a Gnostic text, made him the hero who obeyed Jesus' secret wish.

a: They weighed out thirty silver coins
p: Only Matthew gives the price. It echoes Zechariah 11:12 and the price of a slave in Exodus.
b: Mark 14:11 says only that they promised money. Matthew names the sum and uses the verb "weighed out" (estēsan), from Zechariah 11:12, where the shepherd of God's flock is paid off with "thirty silver" coins, an insulting wage, and told to throw it "to the potter" in the house of the LORD. Matthew returns to this text when Judas throws the money back (27:3–10). In the law, thirty shekels of silver is the price paid for a slave gored by an ox: "its owner gives the slave's master silver, thirty shekels" (Exodus 21:32). The silver coins of Jerusalem's Temple were usually Tyrian shekels.

a: the first day of the Feast of Unleavened Bread
t: Was the Last Supper a Passover meal?
p: Matthew, Mark and Luke make it the Passover meal. John places the crucifixion as the lambs were killed.
b: In Matthew, Mark and Luke the Last Supper is the Passover meal, eaten on the evening that began 15 Nisan, and Jesus dies the next afternoon. In John the leaders have not yet eaten the Passover when Jesus is tried (John 18:28), and he dies on "Preparation Day for the Passover" (John 19:14), the hour the lambs were slaughtered. Proposals: (1) the first three Gospels are right, and John has moved the day to show Jesus as the Passover lamb; (2) John is right, and the Supper was a farewell meal with Passover themes (many historians); (3) both are right, because different groups used different calendars (Annie Jaubert, who argued for a Tuesday supper on the solar calendar known from Jubilees and Qumran); (4) John's phrases can be read to fit the Synoptic date (Craig Blomberg, D. A. Carson). Joachim Jeremias listed many features of the Supper that fit a Passover meal.
r: Mark 14:12; Luke 22:7–15; John 13:1; John 18:28; John 19:14; John 19:31; 1 Corinthians 5:7; 1 Corinthians 11:23

p: Matthew uses a Greek word for an unnamed person. The host stays anonymous.
b: Ton deina is the Greek way of saying "so-and-so," a person one does not name. Mark 14:13–15 and Luke 22:10–12 tell instead of a man carrying a water jar who leads the disciples to a large upstairs room. Why the secrecy? Perhaps to protect the host, or to keep Judas from knowing the place in advance. Matthew keeps the man nameless but keeps Jesus in command: "The Teacher says."

p: Kairos is the appointed moment. Jesus sees his death as the hour God has set.
b: Kairos means a fitting or appointed time, not clock time. The demons asked whether Jesus had come "before the time" (8:29); now the time has come near, as he will say in Gethsemane, "the hour has come near" (26:45). John's Gospel speaks the same way of Jesus' "hour" (John 2:4; 12:23; 13:1; 17:1). Jesus goes to his death knowingly, not as a victim of chance.

p: At a formal meal people lay on couches, leaning on the left elbow. At Passover even the poorest reclined.
b: Paintings such as Leonardo's Last Supper seat everyone on one side of a table. At a formal Greek, Roman or Jewish meal people lay on cushions or couches around a low table, leaning on the left arm and eating with the right. The Mishnah says that on Passover night "even the poorest in Israel must not eat until he reclines" (Mishnah Pesachim 10:1), because free people recline and slaves stand. That is how the beloved disciple could lean back against Jesus (John 13:23–25).

a: dipped his hand in the bowl
p: Sharing a dish made betrayal worse. John links this with Psalm 41:9.
b: Everyone at the table dipped bread into the shared bowl of sauce, so the words do not point to one man; they stress that the traitor is a table friend. To eat together was a bond of trust. John 13:18 quotes Psalm 41:9 here: "Even the man I was at peace with, the one I trusted, / who ate my bread, / has raised his heel high against me." Matthew adds, alone of the Gospels, Judas's own question and Jesus' reply (26:25).

a: just as it stands written about him
t: Planned by God, chosen by Judas
p: Jesus says his death fulfills Scripture, yet Judas is still responsible. Matthew holds both at once.
b: No single passage is named. Christians have pointed to Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, Psalm 41:9 and Daniel 7. The verse holds two things together: the Son of Man "goes" as God planned, yet "woe" to the man who hands him over. Jewish thought of the time could say both; the Mishnah says "all is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is given" (Mishnah Avot 3:15). Christians have long argued over how far God's plan and Judas's choice fit together. Augustinians and Calvinists stress God's sovereign purpose working through evil choices; Arminian and Orthodox readers stress that God foreknew but did not cause Judas's act.

p: A yes, but a guarded one: the words are yours, not mine. Jesus answers the high priest and Pilate the same way.
b: Sy eipas, "you said," appears again before the high priest (26:64), and sy legeis, "you say," before Pilate (27:11). Most scholars take it as a real but reserved yes: "The words are yours," leaving the speaker to face what he has said. Rabbinic texts show a similar reply in sensitive matters. Some think it is less than a yes ("That is your way of putting it"). Here Judas, who calls Jesus "Rabbi" rather than "Lord" (contrast 26:22), names himself with his own question.

p: A Jewish blessing over bread thanks God, not the bread. The Byzantine text says "gave thanks."
b: Eulogēsas, "having blessed," refers to the blessing every Jewish meal began with. Its object is God. The Mishnah gives the ending of the blessing over bread: "who brings forth bread from the earth" (Mishnah Berakhot 6:1). Over the cup, Jesus "gave thanks" (eucharistēsas, 26:27), from which comes the word "Eucharist." The two verbs mean nearly the same thing. Many later manuscripts read "gave thanks" over the bread too (see the variant). The four actions, took, blessed, broke, gave, also appear at the feedings of the crowds (14:19; 15:36), and shaped the order of Christian worship.

p: Four short words have divided the churches more than almost any others. The Where Christians differ card sets the views side by side.
b: The Greek touto estin to sōma mou is plain: "this is my body." Jesus probably spoke Aramaic, which would not need the word "is" (perhaps den gufi or den bisri). What the words mean has been argued since the Reformation. Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran Christians read them as a real presence of Christ's body; Reformed Christians as a real but spiritual feeding on Christ by faith; Zwingli and most Baptists as a sign that represents and remembers him. At a Passover meal, the head of the family explained the foods ("this is the bread of affliction that our ancestors ate"), so some scholars read Jesus' words as a new explanation of the meal. Matthew alone adds "eat" to "take," and "Every one of you, drink from it" (26:27).

p: Jesus echoes Moses at Sinai, who splashed blood on the people to seal the covenant.
b: At Mount Sinai, Moses sealed God's covenant with Israel with sacrificial blood: "Here is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has cut with you on the terms of all these words" (Exodus 24:8). Jesus applies those words to his own blood. Jeremiah 31:31 had promised a "new covenant" written on the heart, and Luke 22:20 and 1 Corinthians 11:25 say "the new covenant in my blood." In Matthew the oldest manuscripts have "my blood of the covenant"; later ones add "new" (see the variant). Drinking blood was forbidden in the law (Leviticus 17:10–14), which is one reason many think Jesus spoke in signs here and others think the shock was intended.
r: Exodus 24:8; Jeremiah 31:31–34; Zechariah 9:11; Hebrews 9:18–22; Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25; Leviticus 17:11

a: It is being poured out for many
p: "Many" echoes Isaiah 53, where the servant bears the sin of many. It means "the multitude," not "some."
b: Isaiah 53:12 says God's servant "emptied out his life to the point of death... He bore the sin of many." Jesus has already said the Son of Man came "to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (20:28). In Hebrew idiom "the many" means the great number, everyone in view, not a limited few (compare Romans 5:15, 18). Christians have still argued over the scope: Reformed theology of "limited" or "particular" atonement reads "many" as the elect; most churches read it as all people. "Poured out" is sacrificial language for blood at the altar (Leviticus 4:7).

a: so that sins can be forgiven
t: Forgiveness moved from John's baptism to the cup
p: Mark says John's baptism was "for the forgiveness of sins." Matthew leaves that out there and puts it here.
b: Mark 1:4 describes John's baptism as "for the forgiveness of sins." Matthew's account of John (3:1–12) leaves those words out, and only here, at the cup, does Matthew use the phrase. Many scholars see a deliberate choice: in Matthew, forgiveness comes through Jesus' death. It fits the angel's word at the start: "he is the one who will save his people from their sins" (1:21). This is one of many small changes that suggest Matthew used Mark and edited it with care, though scholars who hold that Matthew wrote first explain it differently.

p: Jesus uses the words of the Jewish blessing over wine. He will not drink again until the kingdom's feast.
b: The Greek genēma tēs ampelou, "produce of the vine," comes from the Jewish blessing over wine: "who creates the fruit of the vine" (Mishnah Berakhot 6:1). At Passover four cups of wine were drunk (Mishnah Pesachim 10:1). Jesus vows not to drink again until "that day," the great feast of the kingdom that Isaiah 25:6 pictures with "aged wines" and that Jesus described when many will come from east and west to eat with Abraham (8:11). Some churches use grape juice and point to this phrase; most Christians through history have used wine.
orig: ἐκ τούτου τοῦ γενήματος τῆς ἀμπέλου

p: The Passover meal ended with the Hallel, Psalms 113–118. Jesus walked to his arrest singing them.
b: The Mishnah describes the Passover meal ending with the second half of the Hallel, the praise Psalms 113–118 (Mishnah Pesachim 10:6–7). If so, among the last words Jesus sang were "A stone that the builders threw out / has become the head of the corner" (Psalm 118:22), which he had quoted against the leaders (21:42), and "I will not die, for I will live / and tell what Yah has done" (Psalm 118:17). The Greek verb means "having sung hymns," without saying which.

a: Every one of you will be tripped up because of me
p: The verb is skandalizō, to trip on a snare. It runs through Matthew.
b: Skandalizō means to trip someone up or to fall into a trap, and so to lose faith or turn away. Jesus warned of it in the parable of the seeds: some fall away "When hardship or persecution comes" (13:21). He also said, "blessed is anyone who is not tripped up because of me" (11:6). Now all of them will be tripped up, including Peter, who says he never will be (26:33). Matthew does not hide the failure of the men who led the church he writes for.

p: Zechariah 13:7 commands a sword to strike God's shepherd. In the Gospels God himself says "I will strike."
b: Zechariah 13:7 in Hebrew reads, in a fresh rendering: "Sword, wake up against my shepherd, against the man who is close to me, declares the LORD of Armies. Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered." The Hebrew has a command; Matthew and Mark have "I will strike," making God the one who acts. Zechariah 9–14 runs through the passion story: the king on a donkey (21:5; Zechariah 9:9), the thirty silver coins (Zechariah 11:12–13), the blood of the covenant (Zechariah 9:11), and the one they pierced (Zechariah 12:10; John 19:37). In Zechariah the scattering leads to a purified remnant who say "The LORD is my God."
r: Zechariah 13:7–9; Zechariah 9:9; Zechariah 11:12–13; Zechariah 12:10; Mark 14:27; John 16:32; 9:36

a: I will get to Galilee ahead of you
p: Even as Jesus predicts desertion, he promises to meet them again. The angel repeats it in 28:7.
b: "Lead the way ahead" (proagō) is a shepherd's word: the scattered sheep will be gathered again. The promise is kept: the angel repeats it (28:7), the risen Jesus repeats it (28:10), and the gospel ends on a mountain in Galilee (28:16). Galilee, "Galilee of the nations" (4:15), is where Jesus began, and where he sends his followers to all the nations.

p: Roosters crowed before dawn. Mark says the rooster would crow twice; Matthew has one crowing.
b: Mark 14:30 says "before a rooster crows twice," and Mark 14:72 records two crowings. Matthew, Luke and John have one. The Romans called the watch from midnight to three in the morning "cockcrow" (compare Mark 13:35), and some think a trumpet signal at the end of that watch was meant. The Mishnah says that chickens were not to be raised in Jerusalem (Mishnah Bava Kamma 7:7), but whether that rule was kept in Jesus' day is unknown. Most readers take a real rooster.

p: The name means "oil press." It was an olive grove on the slope of the Mount of Olives.
b: Gethsemane comes from Aramaic gat shemanim, "press of oils." It lay on the lower western slope of the Mount of Olives across the Kidron Valley from the Temple. John 18:1 calls it a garden and says Jesus often met his disciples there (John 18:2). The traditional site, with ancient olive trees beside the Church of All Nations, fits the description, though the exact spot is not certain. Christian writers have seen meaning in the name: the place where olives were crushed for oil is where Jesus was crushed in prayer.

t: The same three, and a cup
p: The three who saw Jesus' glory on the mountain now see his anguish. Two of them had claimed they could drink his cup.
b: Peter, James and John saw Jesus transfigured (17:1–8). Now they see him in grief. James and John, "Zebedee's two sons," are the ones whose mother asked for seats at Jesus' right and left, and who told him, "We can" drink his cup (20:20–23). Here they cannot even stay awake while he prays about that cup. When Jesus is "enthroned" on the cross, the places at his right and left go to two bandits (27:38).

a: My soul is crushed with grief, enough to kill me
p: Jesus speaks in the words of the Psalms. The grief is real, not acted.
b: The word perilypos, "deeply grieved," is the word the Greek Old Testament uses in the refrain of Psalms 42–43: "Why are you so bowed down, my soul? / Why do you groan within me?" (Psalm 42:5). "Enough to kill me" (literally "to death") recalls Jonah's "it is right for me to be angry, to death" (Jonah 4:9). Early Christians used this scene against those who said Jesus only seemed human: he had a human soul that could be troubled. Maximus the Confessor (died 662) used Gethsemane to argue that Christ had a human will as well as a divine one, the teaching the Third Council of Constantinople adopted in 681.
orig: περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου
r: Psalm 42:5; Psalm 42:11; Psalm 43:5; Jonah 4:9; Mark 14:34; John 12:27; Hebrews 5:7

a: let this cup go past me
p: In the prophets, God makes the guilty drink a cup of his anger. Jesus prays to be spared it, and accepts it.
b: In the Old Testament "the cup" often stands for God's judgment, which the guilty must drink (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17, 22; Jeremiah 25:15–17). Jesus asked James and John if they could drink his cup (20:22), and at supper he gave his disciples the cup of his blood (26:27). Christians have read the prayer in different ways: Jesus shrinks from death itself, as any human would; or from bearing God's judgment on sin; or both. Matthew stresses obedience. The second prayer, "may your will be done" (26:42), uses the very words of the Lord's Prayer.

p: Jesus prays the prayer he taught: Father, your will be done, and keep us from testing.
b: Mark 14:36 has the Aramaic "Abba, Father." Matthew writes "My Father," and his Gethsemane scene echoes the prayer Jesus taught (6:9–13) phrase by phrase: "Father"; "May your will be done" (26:42, word for word as 6:10); and "do not bring us into testing" behind the warning "so that you do not walk into testing" (26:41; 6:13). The one who taught the prayer prays it in the hour of trial.

a: The spirit is eager, the flesh weak.
p: This is not soul against body. It contrasts a willing heart with human frailty.
b: In Jewish thought "flesh" is human nature in its weakness, not the body as bad and the soul as good. "Spirit" may be the human spirit, eager to stay loyal, or the Spirit of God working in people (the phrase recalls Psalm 51:12, "let a generous spirit hold me up"). Later rabbis spoke of two inclinations in every person, the good and the evil (yetzer). Jesus' words are not a scolding excuse but a warning: good intentions are not enough without prayer. "Testing" (peirasmos) is the same word as in the Lord's Prayer, "do not bring us into testing" (6:13).
orig: τὸ μὲν πνεῦμα πρόθυμον ἡ δὲ σὰρξ ἀσθενής

a: Go on, sleep now and rest.
p: The Greek can be read as an order, a sad question, or irony. Jesus then says, "Get up."
b: Katheudete loipon kai anapauesthe can be punctuated three ways. As a command, "Sleep on now and take your rest" (KJV): the time for watching is over. As a question, "Are you still sleeping and resting?": a reproach. Or as irony. Since Jesus at once says, "Get up, let's go," many read it as a question or as weary irony. Ancient Greek manuscripts had no question marks, so translators must choose.

a: a big crowd carrying swords and clubs
p: Matthew says the crowd was sent by the chief priests and elders. John adds Roman soldiers.
b: The arresting party was probably the Temple police and servants of the high priest, armed with short swords and clubs. John 18:3, 12 adds a cohort of Roman soldiers and their commander, which may mean Pilate had agreed in advance. A night arrest outside the city avoided the crowds the leaders feared (26:5).

p: Chaire was the everyday greeting. In Matthew only Judas calls Jesus "Rabbi."
b: Chaire literally means "rejoice," but it was the normal word for hello. The soldiers use it in mockery, "Hail, King of the Jews!" (27:29), and the risen Jesus greets the women with its plural (28:9). In Matthew the other disciples call Jesus "Lord" (26:22); only Judas calls him "Rabbi" (26:25, 49). Jesus had told his followers not to be called rabbi, "Your Teacher is one" (23:8). The title is respectful, but in Matthew it marks distance.

p: A disciple greeted a teacher with a kiss. Scripture remembers a kiss that led to murder.
b: A kiss on the cheek was a normal greeting, especially of a respected teacher. The verb here (kataphileō) is stronger than the one in 26:48 and can mean to kiss warmly or repeatedly. Readers have long heard Joab, who took Amasa by the beard "to kiss him" and stabbed him (2 Samuel 20:9–10), and the proverb: "Wounds from someone who loves you are true, / but kisses from someone who hates you come thick and fast" (Proverbs 27:6). In Luke 22:48 Jesus asks, "Judas, are you handing over the Son of Man with a kiss?"

a: Friend, get on with what you came for.
p: The Greek is clipped and unclear. It may be an order, a question, or an exclamation.
b: Hetaire, eph' ho parei is literally "Friend, for what you are here." It may be a command ("do what you came for"), a question ("why are you here?", KJV "wherefore art thou come?"), or an exclamation ("so this is what you are here for!"). Most modern scholars prefer the command: Jesus remains in control. "Friend" (hetairos, "comrade, mate") is used in Matthew only for people in the wrong: the grumbling worker (20:13) and the guest without wedding clothes (22:12).

p: Matthew leaves the swordsman nameless. John names Peter and the slave Malchus; Luke says Jesus healed him.
b: All four Gospels tell this. Mark 14:47 calls the swordsman "one of those standing by." John 18:10 names him as Simon Peter and the slave as Malchus. Luke 22:51 alone says Jesus touched the ear and healed it. Matthew alone gives Jesus' saying about the sword (26:52–54).

a: Everyone who takes the sword will be destroyed by the sword.
p: A proverb-like saying that pacifist churches read as a rule for all Christians. Others read it as a word for that night.
b: The saying sounds like Genesis 9:6: "Whoever spills a human's blood, / by a human his blood will be spilled" and is echoed in Revelation 13:10: "If anyone is to be killed by the sword, by the sword they must be killed." Anabaptists, Quakers and other peace churches read it, with 5:38–48, as forbidding Christians to use violence. Churches that teach just war read it as Jesus forbidding armed defense of himself, since his path was the cross, while government still "bears the sword" (Romans 13:4). See the Where Christians differ card for this chapter.

a: more than twelve legions of angels
p: A Roman legion had about 5,000 to 6,000 soldiers. Jesus could summon armies of angels, one legion for each apostle and more.
b: A legion was the main unit of the Roman army, at this time about five or six thousand men. Twelve legions would be some seventy thousand angels, perhaps one legion for each of the eleven disciples and Jesus. The Roman garrison in Judea was much smaller than a single legion. In the testing in the wilderness Jesus refused to call on angels to save himself (4:6–7, 11), and he refuses again.

p: A lēstēs was an armed robber, and Josephus uses the word for violent rebels against Rome.
b: Lēstēs means bandit, highwayman. Josephus uses it often for the armed rebels in Judea before and during the war with Rome. The same word describes the two men crucified with Jesus (27:38, 44), and John 18:40 calls Barabbas one. Jesus protests that he taught openly "in the Temple" every day. The irony is that the man treated as a rebel dies between two of them, under a placard that calls him a king.

a: All this has happened so that the writings of the prophets would be fulfilled.
p: The line may end Jesus' speech or be Matthew's comment. Either way, no single prophet is named.
b: Matthew has used fulfillment formulas since 1:22. Most translations put this line in Jesus' mouth, as the end of his reply to the crowd (Mark 14:49 has "But it is so that the Scriptures would be fulfilled"). Some scholars read it as Matthew's own comment, like his other formulas. It names no passage; it covers the whole story, from Zechariah's struck shepherd (26:31) to Isaiah's servant. Then comes the hardest line for the disciples: "they all abandoned him and ran off," as 26:31 foretold.

p: The Sanhedrin was Jerusalem's high council. Whether this night hearing was a formal trial is debated.
b: The Sanhedrin was the high council of priests, elders and scribes, led by the high priest; the Mishnah says the great Sanhedrin had seventy-one members (Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6). The Mishnah's rules forbid a capital trial at night or on the eve of a festival, require a second day before a guilty verdict, and define blasphemy narrowly (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:1, see also 5:5; and 7:5 on blasphemy). Matthew's night trial breaks these rules. Views: (1) the leaders broke their own law; (2) the Mishnah, written down about AD 200 by rabbis in the Pharisees' tradition, does not show the rules of a Sadducee-led court in AD 30; (3) this was an informal hearing to prepare a charge for Pilate, as John 18:13–24 suggests, and Luke 22:66 puts the council meeting in the morning. Many historians, including Raymond Brown and E. P. Sanders, hold some form of (2) or (3).

a: I am able to tear down God's sanctuary and build it in three days.
p: Matthew calls it false testimony, yet something like it goes back to Jesus. John 2:19 has a version.
b: The law required two witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15), and Matthew says two came. Their charge echoes Jesus' prediction that the Temple would be torn down (24:2) and a saying John records: "Tear this temple down, and within three days I will raise it" (John 2:19), which John explains as his body. Matthew softens Mark's version (Mark 14:58, "this sanctuary that human hands made... another that no hands made") to "I can." To threaten the Temple was serious: Jeremiah was nearly killed for it (Jeremiah 26:8–11), and Stephen was charged with it (Acts 6:14). The mockers repeat it at the cross (27:40), and at Jesus' death the sanctuary's curtain tears (27:51).

p: The high priest invokes God and demands an answer. Jesus, who said "do not swear," answers.
b: Exorkizō means to put someone under oath by naming God. The law obliged a witness under such an oath to speak (Leviticus 5:1: "he hears the public curse calling for witnesses... but he does not tell. Then he will carry his guilt"). Jesus, who had kept silent (compare Isaiah 53:7), now answers. Churches that allow oaths in court (for example the Westminster Confession, chapter 22) point to this; Anabaptists and Quakers, who refuse oaths because of 5:33–37, note that Jesus himself does not swear but simply answers.
orig: Ἐξορκίζω σε κατὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τοῦ ζῶντος

a: the Messiah, the Son of God
t: Peter's confession on an enemy's lips
p: The high priest uses the very words of Peter's confession in 16:16, as an accusation.
b: Peter said, "You are the Messiah, the Son of the living God" (16:16). Now the high priest asks, "by the living God," whether Jesus is "the Messiah, the Son of God." In Jewish usage "son of God" could be a title of Israel's king (Psalm 2:7: "You are my son. / This day I have fathered you"; 2 Samuel 7:14), so the two titles could mean the same thing. Christians later heard more in it. Matthew places the confession of the disciple and the accusation of the judge side by side.

a: sitting at the Power's right hand and coming on the clouds of the sky
p: Jesus answers with two Scriptures: the king seated at God's right hand, and the son of man coming with clouds.
b: Jesus joins Psalm 110:1, where the LORD tells "my lord" to sit at his right hand (already used in 22:41–46), with Daniel 7:13: "with the clouds of heaven one like a son of man was coming, and he reached the Ancient of Days" (a fresh rendering of the Aramaic). "The Power" is a reverent way of saying God without naming him; later rabbis also called God ha-Gevurah, "the Might." "From now on" is Matthew's addition: the vindication begins at once, with the resurrection (28:18). Some readers take "coming on the clouds" as Jesus' return; others, such as R. T. France and N. T. Wright, read it as his going up to God to receive authority, as in Daniel, seen in the events that followed, including the fall of the Temple in AD 70.

p: The high priest tears his robe, as the rules required for blasphemy. But what had Jesus said that was blasphemy?
b: The Mishnah says judges who heard blasphemy repeated in court were to stand and tear their garments, and defines the blasphemer as one who pronounces the divine name itself (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:5). Jesus did not say the Name; he said "the Power." Claiming to be the Messiah was not blasphemy either: others did so. Scholars suggest the charge was (1) claiming to sit beside God and share his throne; (2) threatening God's Temple; (3) a broader sense of insulting God and his leaders. In Matthew the reader knows the irony: the judge accuses of blasphemy the one who truly is God's Son, and soon people "insult" (literally "blaspheme") Jesus at the cross (27:39).

t: A small clue to the Synoptic puzzle
p: Without a blindfold the taunt makes little sense. Luke has the same words, which Mark lacks.
b: In Mark 14:65 they cover Jesus' face and say "Prophesy!" In Matthew there is no blindfold, so the question "Who struck you?" seems pointless. Yet Luke 22:64 has the very same question, the same five Greek words (tis estin ho paisas se), which Mark does not. This is the best-known "minor agreement" of Matthew and Luke against Mark. Scholars who hold that Matthew and Luke used Mark independently explain it by a copyist's harmonizing or a shared oral form; Mark Goodacre and others who follow the Farrer theory see it as evidence that Luke knew Matthew.

a: You too were with Jesus the Galilean
p: Peter's denials grow: before all, then with an oath, then with curses. Jesus had said whoever denies him will be denied.
b: The three scenes build: first a slave girl, then another girl at the gate, then the bystanders. Peter's answers grow too: a plain denial "with all of them listening," then an oath, then curses (26:70, 72, 74). Meanwhile, inside, Jesus is under oath and tells the truth (26:63–64). Jesus had said, "whoever denies me in front of people, I too will deny that person in front of my Father in heaven" (10:33). Peter's tears and restoration (28:10, 16) show that the failure was not the end. The early church kept this story, which shamed its leading apostle, which many historians count as a sign that it happened.

p: The Greek is Nazōraios, the word of 2:23. Here it is a label of contempt from a stranger.
b: Nazōraios means "from Nazareth" and is the word behind "He will be called a Nazarene" (2:23; see the note there). Nazareth was a small, unknown village (John 1:46). The first girl called Jesus "the Galilean"; the second, "the Nazarene": a man from nowhere. Jews later called Christians Notzrim, "Nazarenes," and the name is still used for Christians in Hebrew and Arabic.

a: The way you talk shows it.
p: Galileans spoke Aramaic with a different accent from Jerusalem. The Talmud jokes about it.
b: Peter's speech, literally his "talk," gave him away. Galilean Aramaic was known for slurring the throat sounds, so that some words ran together. The Babylonian Talmud tells a joke about a Galilean in the market whose words for "donkey," "wine," "wool" and "lamb" could not be told apart (Eruvin 53b). Matthew alone mentions the accent.

p: The verb has no object. Peter may curse himself if he lies, or he may curse Jesus.
b: Katathematizein means to call down a curse. Most translations add "on himself": Peter swears, "May God curse me if I know him." But the Greek has no object, and some scholars think Peter cursed Jesus, which is what Roman officials later demanded of accused Christians. About AD 112, Pliny the Younger wrote that he released those who "cursed Christ," which he said real Christians could not be forced to do (Pliny, Letters 10.96). Matthew's readers may have heard Peter's fall in that light.

a: He went outside and cried bitterly.
p: Both failed Jesus that night. Peter wept and was restored; Judas regretted and despaired. Tradition sets them side by side.
b: Matthew tells Peter's tears and then, at once, Judas's end (27:3–5), and Christians have always read them together. Both turned against Jesus; both were sorry. Peter waited, was met again by the risen Lord, and led the church. Judas returned the money to the priests rather than going back to Jesus. Church fathers such as John Chrysostom held up Peter's tears as the model of repentance and warned against Judas's despair. "Bitterly" may echo Isaiah 22:4 in the Greek, "I will weep bitterly."

p: A second meeting at dawn turned the night hearing into a charge to take to the Roman governor.
b: Matthew, like Mark 15:1, has the leaders meet again at daybreak. Luke 22:66 puts the only council session in the morning. The Jewish authorities under Rome could not carry out a death sentence on their own, according to John 18:31, though scholars debate how strict that limit was (stonings did happen, as of Stephen in Acts 7 and James the Lord's brother in AD 62, Josephus, Antiquities 20.200). They needed a charge that a Roman would act on: a man claiming to be "King of the Jews."

p: Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36. An inscription with his name was found at Caesarea in 1961.
b: Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect of Judea from about AD 26 to 36. A stone found in the theater at Caesarea Maritima in 1961 names him as "prefect of Judea" and records a building he dedicated to the emperor Tiberius. Philo, a Jewish writer of the time, calls him stubborn and harsh and accuses him of bribes, insults, and executions without trial (Philo, On the Embassy to Gaius 299–305). Josephus tells of Pilate bringing images of the emperor into Jerusalem and using Temple money for an aqueduct (Jewish War 2.169–177). The Roman historian Tacitus records that Christ "suffered the death penalty under Tiberius, at the hands of the procurator Pontius Pilate" (Annals 15.44). The creeds name him for that reason: "crucified under Pontius Pilate."

p: Matthew uses metamelomai, "to regret," not the usual word for repentance. Whether Judas repented is debated.
b: The usual New Testament word for repentance is metanoeō, "to change one's mind and life." Matthew uses metamelomai, "to feel regret, change one's mind," which he also uses of the son who later went to work in the vineyard (21:29, 32), so it is not always a weak word. Judas admits his sin, returns the money and declares Jesus innocent. Many church fathers held that his sin was despair, not seeking mercy. Origen and some modern readers have been more hopeful, and William Klassen (Judas: Betrayer or Friend of Jesus?, 1996) argued that later tradition blackened him. Matthew passes no sentence, but 26:24 is grim.

p: Blood runs through chapter 27: innocent blood, the price of blood, the Field of Blood, Pilate's hands, the people's cry.
b: Judas's phrase recalls the law about an unsolved murder, where the elders pray: "Do not lay innocent blood on your people Israel" (Deuteronomy 21:8), and Jeremiah's warning, "you are bringing innocent blood on yourselves, on this city and on everyone who lives in it" (Jeremiah 26:15). Matthew repeats the word "blood" five times in this chapter (27:4, 6, 8, 24, 25). Jesus had warned that "all the righteous blood poured out on the earth will come on you" (23:35), and at supper he had called his own blood "poured out for many" (26:28). Matthew lets these meanings sit side by side.

a: That's for you to see to.
p: The priests brush Judas off with words Pilate will soon use of them.
b: Sy opsē, literally "you will see," means "that is your problem." In 27:24 Pilate says the same to the crowd with the plural: hymeis opsesthe. Each party in turn tries to push responsibility for Jesus' blood onto someone else. Matthew's repetition invites the reader to notice that none of them can.

p: The word is naos, the inner sanctuary only priests could enter. The scene echoes Zechariah 11:13.
b: Matthew uses naos, the sanctuary building itself, not hieron, the Temple courts. Only priests could enter it, so Judas may have hurled the coins toward it, or Matthew may use the word loosely. Either way it fulfills Zechariah 11:13, where the prophet takes the thirty silver coins and "threw it to the house of the LORD, to the potter." The same word naos is used of the sanctuary Jesus was accused of threatening (26:61) and whose curtain tears at his death (27:51).

a: Then he went and hanged himself.
p: Acts says Judas fell headlong and burst open. Readers harmonize the two or treat them as separate traditions.
b: Acts 1:18–19 says Judas bought a field with his reward, fell headlong, burst open, and the field was called Akeldama, "Field of Blood," because of his blood. Matthew says he hanged himself and the priests bought the field, named for the "price of blood." Harmonizers suggest that the priests bought it in his name and that the body fell when the rope or branch broke. Many critical scholars see two independent traditions that agree on a violent death and a field called Field of Blood. Papias, in the early 100s, told a third, gruesome version in which Judas swelled until he burst. Matthew's wording recalls Ahithophel, David's counselor who betrayed him: "He gave orders for his household, then hanged himself" (2 Samuel 17:23), the only suicide by hanging in the Old Testament.

p: The Greek is korbanas, the Temple fund called "the korban." Josephus says Pilate once raided it.
b: Korbanas comes from Hebrew korban, "offering" (compare Mark 7:11). It was the sacred treasury where offerings were kept. Josephus says Pilate took money from "the sacred treasure called Corbonas" to build an aqueduct, which caused a riot (Jewish War 2.175). The priests' scruple here comes from Deuteronomy 23:18, which forbids bringing a prostitute's wages into the LORD's house: money tainted by sin could not be offered. Matthew lets the irony stand. They will not put blood money in the treasury, but they paid it out in the first place.

p: Tradition places it in the Valley of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem. The name became English for a paupers' graveyard.
b: Since at least the 300s, Christians have located the field at Akeldama in the lower Valley of Hinnom, where many ancient tombs have been found. That valley is where Jeremiah broke a potter's jar and said Topheth would become a graveyard (Jeremiah 19). A field "for strangers" would bury pilgrims and foreigners who died in the city with no family tomb. In English, "potter's field" came to mean any public burial ground for the poor and unknown.

p: Most of the quotation is from Zechariah 11. Why does Matthew name Jeremiah?
b: The thirty silver coins and the potter come from Zechariah 11:12–13, yet Matthew names Jeremiah. Explanations: (1) Matthew blends Zechariah with Jeremiah, who visits a potter (Jeremiah 18), buys a clay jar and speaks of innocent blood and a burial ground in the Valley of Hinnom (Jeremiah 19), and buys a field for silver (Jeremiah 32:6–15); he names the greater prophet, as Mark 1:2 names Isaiah for a blend of Malachi and Isaiah. (2) In one Jewish order of the prophets Jeremiah came first (Babylonian Talmud, Bava Batra 14b), so the scroll may have gone by his name. (3) Jerome reported a Hebrew writing of Jeremiah, shown him by a Nazarene, that had these words; Origen also guessed at a lost writing. (4) A slip of memory. (5) Augustine knew that some copies lacked the name, but held that the original said Jeremiah: the Holy Spirit let the name stand to show that the prophets speak with one voice, so that words of Zechariah are also words of Jeremiah (Harmony of the Gospels 3.7). A few manuscripts change the name to Zechariah or Isaiah or leave it out (see the variant). Most scholars hold (1).

a: just as the Lord had instructed me
t: Matthew's own wording of the prophecy
p: Matthew's quotation matches neither the Hebrew nor the Greek of Zechariah. He shapes it to the story.
b: Zechariah 11:13 in Hebrew says, in a fresh rendering: "The LORD said to me, 'Throw it to the potter, the fine price at which I was priced by them.' So I took the thirty silver and threw it into the house of the LORD, to the potter." Matthew changes "I took" to "they took," "threw to the potter" to "paid them out for the Potter's Field," and adds "as the Lord had instructed me," a phrase common in Exodus. Ancient Jewish interpreters often reshaped a text to bring out how it applied. "The Lord" stands where the Hebrew has the divine name; Greek has no way to show the name.

a: So you are the King of the Jews?
p: To a Roman, a man called king without Rome's approval was a rebel. The title frames the whole trial.
b: The title appears first on the lips of the foreign magi (2:2) and then on Pilate's, the soldiers' and the placard on the cross (27:29, 37). Jews would say "King of Israel" (27:42). Rome appointed client kings like Herod; anyone else claiming the title was guilty of treason against the emperor (maiestas). Whatever the Jewish leaders meant by "Messiah," this is the political form in which the charge reached Pilate. Jesus' reply, "You are the one saying it," is a guarded yes (see the note on 26:25).

a: Jesus did not reply to him with even one word
p: Jesus' silence before his accusers recalls the servant in Isaiah 53, who did not open his mouth.
b: Isaiah 53:7 says of God's servant: "He was mistreated, and he bowed under it, / yet he did not open his mouth. / Like a lamb that is taken off to slaughter, / like a ewe that falls silent in front of her shearers, / he did not open his mouth." Jesus is silent before Caiaphas (26:63) and before Pilate, except for brief words that admit the title. The early church applied this passage to Jesus explicitly (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Peter 2:23). Pliny the Younger later describes asking accused Christians three times before he sentenced them (Letters 10.96); an accused man who would not defend himself puzzled a governor.

a: At the festival the governor used to set one prisoner free
p: No source outside the Gospels mentions this custom. Historians are divided on it.
b: All four Gospels report it (Mark 15:6; John 18:39 calls it "your custom"), but no Roman or Jewish source does. Possible support: the Mishnah allows a Passover lamb to be slaughtered for someone "whom they have promised to bring out of prison" (Mishnah Pesachim 8:6), and a papyrus from Egypt of AD 85 records a governor telling an accused man that he deserved flogging but was handed over to the crowds. Some historians think a one-time pardon was later remembered as a custom; others accept a local practice. Raymond Brown judged that the release of Barabbas is likely historical even if the custom is uncertain.

p: Barabbas means "son of the father." Some manuscripts give his first name as Jesus, a common name.
b: Bar-abba is Aramaic for "son of the father" (or of a man named Abba). In some manuscripts, including Origen's copies, his own name is Jesus: "Jesus Barabbas" (see the variant). If original, Pilate's question is sharp: which Jesus, the son of the father, or the one called Messiah, whom God called "my Son" (3:17)? Origen thought a sinner should not bear the name Jesus, and scribes may have removed it for that reason. Jesus (Yeshua) was one of the most common names of the time. Mark 15:7 says Barabbas was in prison with rebels who had committed murder in the uprising; Matthew calls him only "famous."

p: Only Matthew tells of her dream. A Gentile woman calls Jesus "righteous"; later tradition made her a saint.
b: God speaks in dreams five times in Matthew's birth story (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22), and here once more, to a Roman woman. She calls Jesus "that righteous man," and Pilate will wash his hands of "this man's blood" (27:24). Matthew lets Gentiles bear witness at the edges of the story: the magi, the centurion of Capernaum, the Canaanite woman, the centurion at the cross (27:54). Later writings gave her the name Procla or Claudia Procula, and the Orthodox and Ethiopian churches honor her as a saint. Some modern scholars think Matthew added the scene; others see no reason to doubt it.

a: talked the crowds into asking for Barabbas
p: This was the crowd at the governor's residence, not necessarily the pilgrims who welcomed Jesus. Matthew's words widen as the scene goes on.
b: Readers often contrast the crowds who shouted "Hosanna" (21:9) with these who shout "Have him crucified!" They need not be the same people. A crowd outside the governor's residence early in the morning, gathered by the chief priests, may have been small and made up of the priests' supporters. Matthew moves from "the crowd" (27:15, 24) and "the crowds" (27:20) to "all the people" (27:25), a phrase with a heavy meaning in his Gospel (see the note there). He blames the leaders for persuading them.

p: Pilate acts out a ritual from the law of Moses, a Jewish sign of innocence on a Roman's hands.
b: Deuteronomy 21:6–7 tells the elders of a town near an unsolved murder to "wash their hands over the cow" and say, "Our hands did not shed this blood, and our eyes did not see it done." The Psalms use the same picture: "In innocence I wash my hands" (Psalm 26:6). Washing one's hands after a death was also known among Greeks and Romans. Only Matthew tells this. Critical scholars often see in it a growing tendency of the Gospels to excuse Rome and blame Jewish leaders; the second-century Gospel of Peter goes further and has Herod and the Jews refuse to wash. Others note Matthew's irony: water cannot clean a judge who gives an innocent man to death, and "washing your hands" of something became an English idiom because of this scene.

p: Pilate uses a formula found in Israel's Scriptures: declaring oneself free of guilt for a death.
b: The Greek athōos eimi apo tou haimatos, "I am guiltless of the blood," follows a biblical formula. David says, "Before the LORD, my kingdom and I are clean of the blood of Abner son of Ner for all time" (2 Samuel 3:28), and the spies tell Rahab, "his blood will be on his own head, and we will be free of blame" (Joshua 2:19). The answer of the people in 27:25 uses the other half of that formula. Many later manuscripts read "this righteous man's blood" (see the variant).
orig: Ἀθῷός εἰμι ἀπὸ τοῦ αἵματος τούτου

t: "All the people": the crowd or the nation?
p: Matthew uses laos, his word for Israel as God's people. How much he meant by it here is fiercely debated.
b: Matthew switches from "crowd" (ochlos) to "people" (laos), the word he uses for Israel as God's people: Jesus will "save his people from their sins" (1:21) and shepherd "my people Israel" (2:6). Many scholars, such as Ulrich Luz, think Matthew means Israel as a whole is speaking at this moment, in his theology if not in history. Others hold that it means only the crowd present, as "all" so often means everyone there. The crowd at the governor's residence was at most a few thousand, and perhaps far fewer; it was not the nation; and Jesus, his disciples, the women at the cross and Joseph of Arimathea were all Jews.

a: His blood on us, and on our children!
t: "His blood on us": meaning and misuse
p: A formula for taking blame for a death, misused for centuries to brand Jews as "Christ-killers." See the deep dive.
b: The Greek has no verb: "His blood on us and on our children." It echoes a biblical formula for accepting blame for a death (Joshua 2:19; 2 Samuel 1:16: "Your blood is on your head"). Readings: (1) the crowd accepts the guilt Pilate refuses, and Matthew sees it fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, a generation later, the "children" (compare 23:35–36); (2) Matthew intends a double meaning: Jesus' blood was "poured out for many, so that sins can be forgiven" (26:28), so the cry is unwittingly a prayer for mercy, as Pope Benedict XVI and others have read it; (3) the line reflects Matthew's bitter conflict with the synagogue after AD 70. From the church fathers on, it was read as a curse on all Jews forever, and it fed persecution. The Catholic Church at the Second Vatican Council (Nostra Aetate 4, 1965) and many other churches have rejected that reading.
r: 23:35–36; 26:28; Joshua 2:19; 2 Samuel 1:16; 2 Samuel 3:28–29; Jeremiah 26:15; Acts 5:28; Acts 18:6; Hebrews 12:24

p: Romans whipped condemned men before crucifixion with a whip tipped with bone or metal. Many died of it.
b: The verb phragelloō comes from Latin flagellum, the scourge. The Roman flogging before crucifixion was brutal: leather straps weighted with bone or metal tore the skin of the back. Josephus says a man was "flayed to the bone with scourges" before a governor (Jewish War 6.304). It weakened victims so that they died faster on the cross. Jesus had predicted it (20:19), and John 19:1 places it earlier in the trial.

p: The Praetorium was the governor's headquarters in Jerusalem. A cohort was a unit of several hundred soldiers.
b: "Praetorium" was the name for a Roman commander's headquarters. In Jerusalem it was probably Herod's palace on the city's western hill, where governors stayed, though tradition since the Middle Ages has placed it at the Antonia fortress beside the Temple, the start of the Via Dolorosa. A cohort (speira) had up to 600 men. Pilate's soldiers were auxiliaries, mostly recruited from non-Jewish towns such as Caesarea and Sebaste, who had little love for Jews and mocked a "King of the Jews."

p: Cloak, crown, scepter, kneeling, "Hail": the soldiers stage a parody of the honors paid to an emperor.
b: The scarlet military cloak stands in for royal purple, the thorny crown for the emperor's wreath, the reed for a scepter, and "Hail, King" mimics "Ave, Caesar." Philo describes a similar mockery in Alexandria in AD 38, when a crowd dressed a poor madman named Carabas as a king to insult the Jewish king Agrippa (Philo, Against Flaccus 36–39). Matthew's readers would see the irony: the mockers give the right title to the true king. Matthew alone mentions the reed in his right hand.

p: The verb is the one used in 5:41 for Roman soldiers forcing civilians to carry their load.
b: Angareuō is a loanword from Persian for forced service to the state. Jesus used it in the Sermon on the Mount: "When someone drafts you into service for one mile, go with him for two" (5:41). Simon came from Cyrene, a city in Libya with a large Jewish community; perhaps he was a pilgrim. Mark 15:21 names his sons Alexander and Rufus, as if Mark's readers knew them, and a Rufus is greeted in Romans 16:13. Condemned men normally carried the crossbeam; the need for help suggests Jesus was too weak after the flogging.

p: Golgotha is Aramaic for "skull." The Latin word is calvaria, which gives English "Calvary."
b: Gulgulta means "skull" in Aramaic, perhaps for the shape of a rocky knoll or because it was a place of execution. The Latin Bible translated it Calvariae locus, the source of "Calvary." It was outside the city wall (John 19:20; Hebrews 13:12) but near a road. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre marks the site venerated since the 300s, and excavations show it was a quarry with tombs outside the wall of Jesus' day. The "Garden Tomb" north of the Damascus Gate, proposed in the 1800s, is a favorite of many Protestants but its tomb is much older than the first century.

p: Matthew's wording echoes Psalm 69:21 in Greek. Mark has wine mixed with myrrh, perhaps a painkiller.
b: Mark 15:23 says "wine mixed with myrrh," which may have dulled the pain. The Talmud says women of Jerusalem gave condemned men wine with frankincense "to confuse their mind" (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 43a), based on Proverbs 31:6: "Give beer to someone who is perishing, / and wine to those who are bitter in spirit." Matthew changes myrrh to "gall" (cholē), the word of the Greek Psalm 69:22 (21 in English), which the site's Plain translates from the Hebrew as "They put poison in my food, / and when I was thirsty they made me drink vinegar." In Matthew the drink becomes part of the mockery, and Jesus refuses it, perhaps because of his vow (26:29), perhaps to die with a clear mind.

p: Matthew describes it in two words. His readers knew what crucifixion was: the slowest and most shameful Roman death.
b: The Gospels give almost no details of the act itself. Rome used crucifixion for slaves, rebels and bandits; Cicero called it "the cruelest and most disgusting punishment" (Against Verres 2.5.165). The victim was tied or nailed to a crossbeam, raised onto an upright post, and left to die of exhaustion and suffocation, often over days. In 1968 the heel bone of a crucified man named Yehohanan was found in a Jerusalem tomb with an iron nail still in it, showing that nails were used and that a crucified Jew could be buried. In Mark's timing (Mark 15:25, 34), Jesus died after about six hours on the cross.

a: shared out his clothes by throwing lots
p: The soldiers' perk fulfills Psalm 22:18. The KJV adds a quotation here that is missing from the oldest manuscripts.
b: Executioners kept the victim's clothes. Matthew describes it in the words of Psalm 22:18: "They hand out my clothes among them, / and over my clothing they throw lots." John 19:23–24 quotes the psalm outright, and some later manuscripts copied that quotation into Matthew, which is why the KJV has it here (see the variant). Psalm 22 shapes the whole scene: the mocking and head-shaking (27:39), the taunt that God should get him free (27:43), and the cry "My God, my God" (27:46).

a: This is Jesus, the King of the Jews.
p: Romans posted the charge for passers-by to read. This one named the crime as kingship.
b: Roman writers mention a placard (titulus) announcing why a man was executed (for example Suetonius, Caligula 32). The four Gospels word it slightly differently; John 19:20 says it was in Aramaic, Latin and Greek, and that the chief priests asked to change it. The "crime" was to be "the King of the Jews," which to Rome meant a rebel and to Matthew's readers meant the truth. Christian art abbreviates the Latin as INRI, Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum (from John 19:19).

a: one on his right and one on his left
p: The words recall the request of Zebedee's sons for the seats at Jesus' right and left in his kingdom.
b: The mother of James and John asked that her sons sit "one on your right and one on your left" in Jesus' kingdom (20:21). Jesus told them those places were for those for whom the Father had prepared them (20:23). Here is his enthronement as "King of the Jews," and the places at his right and left go to two bandits. Matthew's readers are meant to see what Jesus' kingdom looks like. Luke 23:40–43 adds that one of them asked to be remembered.

a: kept reviling him. They shook their heads
t: Mocked in the words of Psalm 22
p: "Insulting" is literally "blaspheming." The head-shaking comes from Psalm 22:7.
b: The verb is blasphēmeō: the man condemned for blasphemy (26:65) is now "blasphemed" himself, insulted as the one God has abandoned. The gesture is from Psalm 22:7: "All who see me make fun of me; / they sneer with their lips and shake their heads." The taunt "tear down the sanctuary" repeats the charge at the trial (26:61).

p: The mockers use the devil's words from the testing in the wilderness: "If you are God's Son."
b: In the wilderness the devil twice began, "If you are God's Son" (4:3, 6), and urged Jesus to use his power for himself. Now passers-by say the same words and urge him to come down from the cross. Jesus refuses again: to save others he does not save himself (27:42). Only Matthew has this exact phrase at the cross, which ties the passion to the testing at the start of Jesus' work.

a: if he takes delight in him
p: The chief priests unknowingly quote Psalm 22. A similar scene is in the Wisdom of Solomon.
b: Psalm 22:8 reads: "Roll it onto the LORD! Let the LORD get him free! / Let the LORD snatch him away, since he takes such delight in him!" In Greek the last words are "if he wants him," which Matthew uses. The Wisdom of Solomon, a Jewish book from about the first century BC that is Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, has the wicked say of the righteous man: "if the righteous man is God's son, he will help him" (Wisdom of Solomon 2:18, a fresh rendering). Matthew alone has "After all, he said, 'I am God's Son.'"

a: darkness lay over the whole land
p: An eclipse cannot happen at Passover's full moon. Readers have seen a miracle, a sign, or both.
b: Passover fell at full moon, when a solar eclipse is impossible. Julius Africanus, writing about AD 220, reports that a historian named Thallus called the darkness an eclipse, and rejects that explanation. Some suggest a dust storm or heavy clouds. Matthew presents a sign from God, recalling the ninth plague, when "darkness upon darkness lay over all the land of Egypt for three days" (Exodus 10:22), and Amos 8:9, where God says "I will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight" (fresh rendering). "Land" (gē) can also mean "earth." The sixth to the ninth hour is about noon to three in the afternoon.

p: Jesus prays the first line of Psalm 22. Christians differ on whether he was truly forsaken.
b: In most manuscripts Matthew gives "Eli" in Hebrew where Mark 15:34 has Aramaic "Eloi"; the rest is Aramaic. Codex Vaticanus and a few others have "Eloi" here too (see the variant). The Hebrew "Eli" also explains why bystanders thought he called Elijah (Eliyyahu). The words are the opening of Psalm 22:1: "My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?" Readings: (1) a real cry of abandonment, as Jesus bears the judgment on sin (Luther, Calvin); (2) a prayer of the whole psalm, which ends in rescue and praise (Psalm 22:22–31), as Jews cited a psalm by its first line; (3) the cry of a human being in real agony, while his union with the Father is not broken (many church fathers, Orthodox teaching). See the Where Christians differ card at Psalm 22. It is the only word from the cross in Matthew and Mark.
r: Psalm 22:1; Psalm 22:22–31; Mark 15:34; Luke 23:46; John 19:30; Hebrews 5:7

p: Jews believed Elijah, who never died, would return, and later stories tell of him rescuing people in trouble.
b: Elijah was taken to heaven without dying (2 Kings 2:11), and Malachi 4:5 promised he would come before the day of the LORD. Popular Jewish belief, found in later rabbinic stories, pictured him as a helper who appears to rescue the righteous in distress. The bystanders' mistake is cruelly ironic for Matthew's readers, who know Jesus said Elijah had already come as John the Baptist (11:14; 17:10–13).

p: Oxos was the cheap vinegary wine soldiers drank. Psalm 69:21 says "they made me drink vinegar."
b: Oxos was wine gone sour, mixed with water as a cheap drink called posca by Roman soldiers and workers. It may have been an act of kindness, or part of the mockery, keeping him alive to see whether Elijah would come. Matthew's readers would hear Psalm 69:21: "when I was thirsty they made me drink vinegar." John 19:28–30 says Jesus said "I am thirsty" and drank it.

p: Matthew does not say Jesus "died" but that he released his spirit, an active verb.
b: Mark 15:37 says Jesus "breathed his last." Matthew writes aphēken to pneuma, "he let go of (or sent away) his spirit," and Luke 23:46 has him pray Psalm 31:5: "Into your hand I place my spirit." Many readers see Matthew stressing that Jesus gave his life rather than having it taken (compare John 10:18). Others see a common way of speaking of death. The word pneuma can mean breath, spirit, or life.

p: God tears the sanctuary's curtain from top to bottom. Readers see open access to God, judgment on the Temple, or both.
b: The sanctuary had two great curtains: one at the entrance and one before the most holy place, where only the high priest entered once a year (Exodus 26:31–33: "The veil will be a dividing line for you between the holy place and the most holy place"). Josephus describes the outer curtain as a Babylonian tapestry embroidered with the heavens (Jewish War 5.212–214). "From top to bottom" shows God's hand. Readings: (1) the way to God's presence is opened by Jesus' death (Hebrews 10:19–20); (2) a sign of judgment on the Temple, which fell in AD 70 (24:2); (3) God "tears his robe" in mourning, as the high priest tore his (26:65). The Talmud records that in the forty years before the Temple's destruction its doors opened by themselves (Babylonian Talmud, Yoma 39b).

a: many bodies of the saints who slept in death were raised
p: Only Matthew tells this. Readers take it as history, as a sign written in prophetic language, or as both.
b: The scene draws on Ezekiel 37:12, where God says, "I am going to open your graves and bring you up from your graves, my people" (a fresh rendering), and Zechariah 14:4–5, where the Lord's feet stand on the Mount of Olives and "all the holy ones" come with him. Readings: (1) a historical event, as most of the church has held; (2) a sign told in the language of Jewish apocalyptic writing to show that Jesus' death begins the resurrection of the end time. Michael Licona suggested (2) in 2010, and the debate that followed among evangelicals (with Norman Geisler and others) showed how sensitive the question is. Church tradition linked it with Christ's descent to the dead and his freeing of the righteous of old, a favorite subject of Eastern icons. "Saints" here means God's holy people of Israel's past.
r: Ezekiel 37:12–14; Zechariah 14:4–5; Daniel 12:2; Isaiah 26:19; 1 Corinthians 15:20–23; 1 Peter 3:18–20; 1 Peter 4:6

t: Raised on Friday, out on Sunday?
p: The order of events is unclear. The words may go with "left the tombs" or with "entered the holy city."
b: Read one way, the saints were raised when Jesus died but stayed in their tombs until his resurrection on Sunday. Read another, they came out at once and entered the city after his resurrection. Greek manuscripts had no commas. Some scholars think "after his resurrection" was added, by Matthew or an early copyist, so that Jesus would remain "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20); no manuscript lacks it. "The holy city" is Jerusalem (4:5).

a: This man really was God's Son!
p: The Greek has no article. A Roman might mean "a divine man"; Matthew means the confession of faith.
b: The Greek theou huios has no "the," so grammatically it can mean "a son of a god," which a pagan soldier might say of a hero. But Greek titles before the verb often drop the article, as in John 1:1, and Matthew surely means the full confession. In Matthew the Father called Jesus "my Son" (3:17; 17:5), the disciples confessed him (14:33; 16:16), the high priest and the mockers used the title as a charge (26:63; 27:40, 43), and now Gentile soldiers confess it in fear. In Matthew, unlike Mark 15:39, the whole guard speaks, moved by the earthquake.

a: These women had followed Jesus from Galilee, serving him
p: The men fled; the women watched. They are the witnesses who link the cross, the burial and the empty tomb.
b: "Followed" is the verb for discipleship, and "served" (diakoneō) is the word for Peter's mother-in-law's service (8:15) and for Jesus' own mission (20:28). Luke 8:1–3 says such women supported Jesus from their own means. The male disciples fled (26:56); the women watch from a distance, see where he is buried (27:61), and are the first at the empty tomb (28:1). Their presence makes them the essential witnesses of the story.

a: Mary the mother of James and Joseph
p: Jesus' brothers were called James and Joseph (13:55). Is this Jesus' mother? Most think not.
b: In 13:55 Jesus' brothers are named "James, Joseph, Simon and Judas." This Mary has sons named James and Joseph. If she were Jesus' mother, Matthew would surely say so. Mark 15:40 calls her "the mother of James the younger and of Joses," and John 19:25 lists "Mary the wife of Clopas." Catholic tradition since Jerome identifies this Mary as the mother of the James and Joseph called Jesus' "brothers," who were therefore his cousins. Many Protestant scholars think the names, very common at the time, show only a coincidence. Orthodox tradition holds that the brothers were Joseph's sons by an earlier marriage. See the topic on Jesus' brothers.

a: had been made a disciple of Jesus
p: Joseph's wealth matters: it fulfills Isaiah's word about a rich man in the servant's death.
b: Only Matthew calls Joseph rich and a disciple; Mark 15:43 calls him a respected council member waiting for the kingdom, and Luke 23:50–51 says he had not agreed with the council's decision. Jesus had said it is hard for a rich man to enter the kingdom (19:23–24); here one does. Isaiah 53:9 says of the servant, "They gave him a burial place among the wicked, / and, in his deaths, with a rich man," The verb mathēteuō, "make a disciple," is the one Jesus uses in the commission (28:19). Arimathea was a town in Judea, perhaps Ramathaim, Samuel's hometown.

a: rolled a great stone up against the door of the tomb
t: A rock-cut tomb and its stone
p: Wealthy Jerusalem families cut tombs in the rock. Round rolling stones were rare; most doors were closed with square blocks.
b: Jerusalem's rich buried their dead in rock-cut tombs with benches or niches; after a year the bones were gathered into a bone box (ossuary). The archaeologist Amos Kloner found that, of more than nine hundred tombs from this period around Jerusalem, only a handful were closed with a round rolling stone; most had a square stone plug. Kloner concluded that Jesus' tomb was most likely closed with a square block, and that the Greek verbs for "roll" fit that too, since such a block was rolled or tumbled into place. Others answer that a round stone, rare as it was, suits a rich man's new tomb. Burial before nightfall followed the law: "his body must not stay on the tree overnight" (Deuteronomy 21:23).
r: Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Isaiah 22:16; Mark 15:46; Mark 16:3–4; Luke 23:53; John 19:41–42

p: Paraskeuē, "Preparation," was the Jewish name for Friday. Matthew means Saturday, the Sabbath, without saying so.
b: Paraskeuē was the day for preparing food and everything else for the Sabbath, and so the Jewish (and modern Greek) name for Friday (compare Mark 15:42). "The day after Preparation" is the Sabbath. Matthew may avoid the word "Sabbath" to keep from saying outright that the chief priests and Pharisees did business with a Gentile governor and sealed a stone on the holy day. This is the only time the Pharisees appear in Matthew's passion story.

p: Planos is one who leads people astray. The charge appears in later Jewish and anti-Christian writing about Jesus.
b: Planos is a deceiver or impostor, one who leads people astray, the kind of false prophet Deuteronomy 13 commands Israel to resist. John 7:12 reports some saying Jesus "leads the crowd astray." Justin Martyr, about AD 155, says Jewish opponents called Jesus "a magician and a deceiver of the people" (Dialogue with Trypho 69), and a passage in the Babylonian Talmud says Yeshu was executed because he "practiced sorcery and enticed Israel" (Sanhedrin 43a). Matthew's readers knew this charge from their own debates.

a: the last deception would be worse than the first
p: The leaders unknowingly echo Jesus' saying about the evil spirit that returns: "the last state is worse than the first."
b: Jesus had said of "this evil generation" that its last state would be worse than the first (12:45). The chief priests now fear that the "last deception," the claim of resurrection, will be worse than the "first," Jesus' claim to be Messiah. The word for deception, planē, matches the "deceiver" (planos) of 27:63. Matthew turns their words into a prophecy: the claim of the resurrection did spread, and they themselves invent the lie (28:13–15).

t: "You have a guard" or "Take a guard"?
p: The Greek can mean either. If Pilate gives Roman soldiers, it explains why the chief priests later protect them from the governor.
b: Echete koustōdian can be read as a statement, "You have a guard" (your own Temple police), or as an order, "Take a guard" (of my soldiers). Koustōdia is a Latin loanword, custodia. Since the soldiers later fear the governor and the priests promise to protect them (28:14), most read it as a Roman guard. The second-century Gospel of Peter expands the story, naming the centurion Petronius.

p: The scene recalls Daniel's den, also sealed with a stone, from which God brought his servant out alive.
b: Seals were pressed into clay or wax across the stone and the doorway, so that any tampering would show. Daniel 6:17 tells how "a stone was brought and set over the mouth of the den, and the king sealed it with his signet ring" (a fresh rendering of the Aramaic), and in the morning Daniel was alive. Christians have long seen the parallel. The guard and seal also answer the claim Matthew mentions in 28:15: no one could have stolen the body.

a: When the Sabbath was over, as light was breaking toward the first day of the week
p: The Greek can mean "late on the Sabbath" or "after the Sabbath." Most take it as Sunday at dawn.
b: Opse sabbatōn normally means "late on the Sabbath," but in later Greek it can mean "after the Sabbath." The next verb, epiphōskō, "to dawn," is used in Luke 23:54 of the Sabbath "beginning" at sunset, since Jewish days begin in the evening. So a few scholars think Matthew means Saturday evening. Most, comparing Mark 16:2 ("Very early... with the sun now up"), take it as dawn on Sunday. "The first day of the week" became the Christian day of worship, "the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10: "It was the Lord's day, and I was in the Spirit").
orig: Ὀψὲ δὲ σαββάτων, τῇ ἐπιφωσκούσῃ εἰς μίαν σαββάτων
r: Mark 16:1–2; Luke 23:54; Luke 24:1; John 20:1; Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2; Revelation 1:10

p: In that culture a woman's testimony counted for little. Historians often say no one would invent women as the first witnesses.
b: In Matthew the women come only "to see" the tomb, not to anoint the body as in Mark 16:1, perhaps because of the guard. Josephus says that in Jewish courts women were not accepted as witnesses (Antiquities 4.219), and the pagan critic Celsus later sneered that the resurrection rested on "a hysterical woman." Yet all four Gospels make women the first to find the tomb empty. Many historians, including N. T. Wright, Richard Bauckham and Dale Allison, argue that early Christians would not have invented witnesses their world found weak. Others answer that the tradition grew in ways we cannot fully trace.

t: The angel of the Lord, at the start and at the end
p: The "angel of the Lord" guided Joseph at Jesus' birth. He returns at the resurrection.
b: Matthew uses "an angel of the Lord" only in the birth story (1:20, 24; 2:13, 19) and here: God's messenger frames the life of Jesus. The angel does not let Jesus out; the stone is rolled away so the women can see that he is already gone. Matthew alone has the earthquake, the angel sitting on the stone, and the guards. The second-century Gospel of Peter goes further and describes Jesus coming out of the tomb, which no New Testament Gospel does.

p: The angel looks like the heavenly figures of Daniel's visions and like Jesus at the transfiguration.
b: In Daniel 7:9 the Ancient of Days wears clothing "white like snow," and in Daniel 10:6 a heavenly man has a face "like the look of lightning" (fresh renderings). At the transfiguration Jesus' clothes became "white as light" (17:2). Matthew paints the angel in the colors of heaven so the reader knows God has acted.

t: The guards become like the dead
p: The men set to guard a corpse become like corpses, while the dead man lives.
b: Matthew's irony is plain: those posted to keep a dead man in his tomb "became as dead men." The same verb, seiō ("shake"), is behind both the earthquake and the guards' trembling. The angel tells the women, "As for you, do not be afraid" (28:5): fear falls on the guards, comfort on the women.

p: Jesus predicted his death and his rising on the third day three times. The angel points back to them.
b: Jesus had said it plainly: he would be killed "and on the third day he would be raised" (16:21; 17:23; 20:19), and he had compared himself to Jonah (12:40). His enemies remembered it (27:63) even when his friends did not. "He has been raised" is a passive verb: God raised him. The New Testament speaks of the resurrection both ways, as God raising Jesus (Acts 2:24) and as Jesus rising (John 10:17–18).

p: Matthew and Mark point to Galilee; Luke and John tell of appearances in Jerusalem. How do they fit?
b: In Matthew the angel and Jesus send the disciples to Galilee, and the only appearance to them is there (28:16–20). Mark 16:7 points to Galilee too. Luke 24 has all the appearances in and near Jerusalem, and tells the disciples to stay in the city (Luke 24:49). John has both, Jerusalem (John 20) and the Sea of Galilee (John 21). Harmonizers suggest appearances in both places over forty days (Acts 1:3). Many critical scholars think different communities kept different traditions. Paul's list of appearances (1 Corinthians 15:5–8) names no places.

a: frightened and full of joy at once
p: Mark ends with the women fleeing in fear and telling no one. Matthew adds joy, and they run to tell.
b: Mark 16:8, the last verse of Mark in the oldest manuscripts, says the women fled "and said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid." Matthew keeps the fear but adds "great joy" and has them run to tell the disciples. This is one of many places where Matthew seems to complete or soften Mark. Joy at the end recalls the magi's joy at the star (2:10).

p: Chairete was the ordinary greeting, but it literally means "rejoice," and these women have every reason to.
