b: Chairete was the everyday "hello" (singular chaire). Most translations say "Greetings." This translation keeps the literal "Rejoice!" here because Matthew has just said the women were "full of joy" (28:8), and because the same word was Judas's greeting with the kiss (26:49) and the soldiers' mockery, "Hail, King" (27:29). The word that was used to betray and mock Jesus now becomes his first word as the risen Lord.

a: held on to his feet, and bowed down before him
t: Holding his feet and bowing down
p: The women touch a real body, not a ghost. They bow down before him, as the magi did at the start, and the word also means worship.
b: Grasping someone's feet was a gesture of humble pleading or homage (2 Kings 4:27). It also shows that the risen Jesus has a body that can be touched (compare Luke 24:39; John 20:27). John 20:17 has Jesus tell Mary Magdalene, "Stop clinging to me." "Bowed down" is proskyneō, to kneel or bow low before someone. It is the bodily act of homage, and it is also the ordinary word for worship: Jesus quotes "Worship the Lord your God" with it (4:10). Matthew uses it of the magi (2:11), of the disciples in the boat (14:33), and of the eleven (28:17). This translation keeps "bow down" in every Gospel scene so that the reader, not the translator, decides how much the act means. Whether it is worship due to God is discussed on the Where Christians differ card for this chapter.

p: The men who abandoned Jesus are now called his brothers. He restores them before they ask.
b: The disciples had fled and Peter had denied him, but the risen Jesus calls them "my brothers." He had said, "Anyone who does what my Father in heaven wants, that person is my brother and my sister and my mother" (12:50), and spoke of "these brothers of mine, even the least of them" (25:40). Hebrews 2:11–12 quotes Psalm 22:22, the turning point of the psalm Jesus prayed on the cross: "I will spread the news of your name to my brothers."

a: a good number of silver coins
p: The story began with thirty silver coins for Judas. It ends with more silver for the soldiers.
b: Matthew uses the same word, argyria, "silver coins," for Judas's payment (26:15; 27:3–9) and for the soldiers' bribe. The leaders paid to have Jesus handed over, and now pay to cover up his resurrection. The "good number" (hikana, "enough") contrasts with the thirty: the lie costs more than the betrayal.

a: His disciples came at night and stole him while we slept.
p: Matthew says this explanation was still told in his day. Justin Martyr reports it a century later.
b: Matthew's story answers a real claim. Justin Martyr, writing about AD 155, says Jewish leaders sent men out to say that "his disciples stole him by night from the tomb" (Dialogue with Trypho 108). Tertullian (about AD 197) mentions another version, that a gardener moved the body (On the Shows 30). Matthew's readers would notice the weakness: if the guards were asleep, how did they know who took him? And Roman soldiers who slept on watch could be put to death. Historians who doubt the resurrection seldom argue for theft today; debate turns rather on the empty tomb and the appearances.

a: among Jews right up to today
p: Matthew writes as if his readers stand apart from "Jews" who tell this story. It hints at a split between church and synagogue.
b: The Greek has no article, "among Jews." Matthew rarely uses "the Jews" in his own voice; elsewhere it appears mostly in "King of the Jews." Here, like his phrase "their synagogues" (4:23; 9:35; 10:17), it suggests that Matthew's Jewish-Christian community had separated from the local synagogue by the time he wrote, probably after AD 70. Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine note that Matthew's polemic belongs to a family quarrel among Jews over who Jesus was, and should not be read as a statement about Jews in general.

a: to the mountain Jesus had appointed for them
p: Matthew's Gospel moves from mountain to mountain. It ends on one, as Moses' life did.
b: Key scenes in Matthew happen on mountains: the testing (4:8), the Sermon (5:1), the healings and feeding (15:29), the transfiguration (17:1), the teaching on the Mount of Olives (24:3). The last scene on a mountain in Galilee recalls Moses, who saw the land from Mount Nebo and commissioned Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:23; 34:1–9). Dale Allison and others see Jesus as a new and greater Moses, who unlike Moses goes with his people. "Eleven" is a quiet reminder of Judas.

p: The Greek may mean "some wavered" or "they wavered." The verb is the one used of Peter sinking in the waves.
b: Hoi de edistasan usually means "but some doubted," but it can mean "but they (all) wavered": they worshiped yet were unsure. The verb distazō appears in the New Testament only here and when Peter sank on the water: "why did you waver?" (14:31). It means hesitation more than unbelief. Matthew's honesty is striking: even at the last meeting not everyone is sure, and Jesus still sends them all.

a: I have been given all authority, in heaven and on earth.
p: The words recall Daniel 7:14, where the son of man is given authority over all peoples.
b: In Daniel 7:14, one like a son of man is given "dominion and honor and a kingdom, and all the peoples, nations and languages will serve him" (a fresh rendering of the Aramaic); the Greek Daniel uses the same word "authority." The devil offered Jesus all the kingdoms of the world if he would worship him (4:8–9); Jesus refused and now receives "all authority" from the Father through the cross. Jesus already had authority to teach and forgive (7:29; 9:6); now it covers heaven and earth. Matthew ends with four "alls": all authority, all the nations, everything I commanded, every day.

a: make all the nations into disciples
t: "All the nations": Gentiles, or Jews too?
p: Jesus once sent the Twelve only to Israel. Now he sends them to all nations. Scholars debate whether Israel is still included.
b: The main verb is mathēteusate, "make disciples"; "go," "baptizing" and "teaching" are participles that say how. Earlier Jesus told the Twelve, "Do not go off on a road to the Gentiles" (10:5–6), and said he was sent only to Israel's lost sheep (15:24). Panta ta ethnē can mean "all the Gentiles" or "all the nations," including Israel. Douglas Hare and Daniel Harrington argued that Matthew means Gentiles only, the mission to Israel being over; John P. Meier and most scholars answer that Israel is included among the nations (compare 24:9, 14; 25:32). The promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed (Genesis 12:3) comes full circle: the Gospel began with "son of Abraham" (1:1).

a: baptizing them into the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit
p: The only place in the Gospels with the Father, Son and Spirit in one formula. Christians read it as the root of the doctrine of the Trinity.
b: "Into the name" (eis to onoma) suggests being placed under the ownership and protection of the one named. The text says one "name" for three: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Didache, a church manual from about AD 100, gives the same words for baptism (Didache 7:1). In Acts people are baptized "in the name of Jesus Christ" (Acts 2:38; 10:48). Some scholars think the triple formula developed in worship and was written into Matthew's ending; others hold that it goes back to the risen Jesus. All Greek manuscripts and early versions have it. Eusebius of Caesarea, before the Council of Nicaea (325), often quoted the verse in a short form, "make disciples of all the nations in my name," which F. C. Conybeare argued in 1901 was the original; most textual critics think Eusebius was paraphrasing. Oneness Pentecostals read the one "name" as Jesus. See the Where Christians differ cards.
r: 3:16–17; Acts 2:38; Acts 8:16; Acts 10:48; Acts 19:5; Romans 6:3–4; 1 Corinthians 1:13–15; 2 Corinthians 13:14; Galatians 3:27

a: teaching them to keep everything I have commanded you
p: Disciples are made by baptism and by teaching. "Everything" points back to the five great speeches.
b: Matthew has gathered Jesus' teaching into five speeches (chapters 5–7, 10, 13, 18, 24–25). Now the disciples, who were taught, become the teachers, like "every scribe who has learned to be a disciple of the kingdom of heaven" (13:52). "Keep" (tēreō) is the language of keeping God's commandments (19:17). Jesus speaks of "what I have commanded," as God commanded Israel through Moses (Deuteronomy 4:2; 12:32). The Lord's teaching, not only belief about him, is the content of the mission.

a: I myself am with you every day
t: God with us, to the end
p: The Gospel ends where it began: Jesus is "Immanuel," God with us (1:23). Matthew has no ascension.
b: In 1:23 Jesus is named "Immanuel," which means "God with us." The last sentence returns to it: "I myself am with you." Scholars call this an inclusio, a frame around the whole book (compare 18:20, "there I am among them"). In the Old Testament God says "I will be with you" when he sends someone on a hard task (Exodus 3:12: "Because I will be with you"; Joshua 1:5; Jeremiah 1:8). Matthew tells no ascension; the book ends with Jesus present, not departing. "Every day" (literally "all the days") and "until the completion of the age" (13:39–40, 49; 24:3) carry the promise to the last day.
